title: Orbital blowout fracture: contents herniate into the maxillary sinus
vignette: A 30-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to left eye pain after being involved in a street fight. He received a fist blow to the left eye and has since had pain and diplopia. Past medical history is notable for 2 previous gunshot wounds. The patient does not smoke cigarettes but has a history of heavy alcohol intake and frequent marijuana use. On examination, there is significant soft tissue swelling around the left eye. Visual acuity is normal, but extraocular motility of the left eye is limited. Pupillary reflexes are normal. A coronal CT scan of the orbits shows a fracture of the left orbital floor with herniation of orbital soft tissue into the air-filled sinus directly below the orbit. The orbital contents of this patient are most likely to herniate into which of the following sites?

clues.text: fist blow to the left eye
clues.note: Blunt trauma to the globe raises intraorbital pressure that fractures the thin surrounding bone - the mechanism of an orbital blowout fracture.
Double vision after eye trauma suggests entrapment/displacement of orbital contents (e.g., inferior rectus) through a blowout fracture.

clues.text: extraocular motility of the left eye is limited
clues.note: Restricted eye movement indicates entrapment of an extraocular muscle/orbital fat in the fracture, typically at the orbital floor.

clues.text: fracture of the left orbital floor with herniation of orbital soft tissue into the air-filled sinus directly below the orbit
clues.note: The orbital floor separates the orbit from the maxillary sinus below; a floor blowout herniates orbital contents into the maxillary sinus.

whatMatters: Blunt globe trauma -> orbital BLOWOUT fracture. The thin orbital FLOOR (over the maxillary sinus) and medial wall (over the ethmoid) are weakest. A floor fracture herniates orbital contents (fat, inferior rectus) INTO THE MAXILLARY SINUS directly below - causing diplopia and restricted upgaze. Answer D.
strategy: Recall orbital wall anatomy: the FLOOR overlies the maxillary sinus and the MEDIAL wall overlies the ethmoid air cells - both are thin and fracture in blowout injuries. A limited-motility floor fracture herniates contents into the maxillary sinus. Reject frontal/sphenoid sinuses (not adjacent to the floor) and inferior conchae (nasal turbinates, not an air-filled sinus).

eliminations.label: Ethmoid air cells - medial wall, not the floor
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the ethmoid air cells lie MEDIAL to the orbit (behind the thin lamina papyracea). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: they are involved in MEDIAL-wall blowouts, but this is a floor fracture herniating INFERIORLY into the maxillary sinus. ✅ Correct if: a medial-wall blowout fracture.

eliminations.label: Frontal sinus - superior, not adjacent to the floor
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the frontal sinus sits in the supraorbital frontal bone ABOVE the orbit. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is not related to the thin orbital floor and is not where floor contents herniate. ✅ Correct if: a supraorbital/frontal bone injury.

eliminations.label: Inferior nasal conchae - turbinates, not an air-filled sinus
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the inferior conchae are part of the nasal turbinate system inside the nasal cavity. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: they are not air-filled sinuses bordering the orbital floor; orbital contents don't herniate here. ✅ Correct if: nasal airflow/turbinate anatomy.

eliminations.label: Sphenoid sinus - posterior, near optic chiasm
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the sphenoid sinus lies POSTERIORLY (anterior to the optic chiasm). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is not in close relation to the orbital floor and is not the herniation site. ✅ Correct if: posterior skull-base/pituitary approaches.

reasoning: Blunt globe trauma raises intraorbital pressure -> blowout fracture of thin orbital walls
The orbital floor (over the maxillary sinus) and medial wall (over the ethmoid) are the weakest
A floor fracture with limited motility herniates orbital contents inferiorly into the maxillary sinus
mechanism: The orbit is bounded by thick bone superiorly (frontal) and laterally (zygoma, sphenoid), but the FLOOR is a very thin plate of maxillary bone separating the orbit from the air-filled MAXILLARY SINUS below, and the MEDIAL wall (lamina papyracea of the ethmoid) is likewise thin. Blunt trauma to the globe (a fist or ball) suddenly raises intraorbital pressure, which is transmitted to these weak walls and fractures them ('blowout fracture') while sparing the globe. Orbital fat and the inferior rectus muscle can herniate/become entrapped through a floor fracture into the maxillary sinus, producing diplopia and restricted vertical eye movement (limited upgaze), sometimes with infraorbital nerve numbness; a fluid level (blood) may appear in the sinus on imaging. Because this is a floor fracture, the herniation site is the maxillary sinus (a medial-wall fracture would herniate into the ethmoid air cells). The frontal and sphenoid sinuses and the inferior conchae do not border the orbital floor.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Anatomy > orbital blowout fracture: thin floor (maxillary sinus) and medial wall (ethmoid); herniation/entrapment of inferior rectus -> diplopia, restricted upgaze, infraorbital numbness.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: A floor fracture herniates orbital contents into the sinus directly below - the maxillary sinus.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on blowout fracture, orbital floor, lamina papyracea, inferior rectus entrapment, or infraorbital nerve? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Ethmoid = medial wall (not floor); frontal/sphenoid sinuses aren't adjacent to the floor; inferior conchae are turbinates, not sinuses.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.text: On the coronal orbital CT: a break in the thin left orbital floor with soft tissue drooping into the maxillary sinus below. Anchor: 'floor blowout -> contents drop into the maxillary sinus.'

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: orbital blowout -> floor (maxillary sinus) or medial wall (ethmoid); inferior rectus entrapment -> restricted upgaze + diplopia.
